expectations.text: Claude does NOT validate the 'VXUS underperformed VTI, therefore skip international' argument — pushes back on this reasoning
expectations.evidence: You are, without knowing it, making a performance-chasing argument... past relative performance between asset classes tells you almost nothing about future relative performance.

expectations.text: Claude explains that 15 years of US outperformance does not predict the next 15 years — cites or implies the alternating cycles of relative performance
expectations.evidence: The prior decade (roughly 2000-2010) ran exactly the opposite way: international stocks significantly outperformed US stocks. An investor in 2010 looking at the prior 10 years would have had the mirror-image argument

expectations.text: Claude makes the valuation argument: US equities are at elevated valuations relative to international, which historically predicts lower relative future returns
expectations.evidence: international equities — particularly Europe and emerging markets — sit at valuations that historically have predicted better forward returns than US equities... much of the US outperformance was driven by valuation expansion, not earnings growth alone

expectations.text: Claude frames a US-only portfolio as an active concentration bet, not a neutral or diversified default
expectations.evidence: When you hold only VTI, you are making an active bet: that the US will continue to outperform every other major economy. That bet might pay off. But it is still a bet against the global market, and you should call it what it is.

expectations.text: Claude recommends adding VXUS (or acknowledges the mainstream Boglehead position favors international), rather than validating the two-fund US-only approach
expectations.evidence: a reasonable allocation would be to take some of that 80% VTI and allocate 15-25% of total equities to VXUS. So something like 55-60% VTI, 20-25% VXUS, 20% BND.
